extracted.intended_audience: news consumers, media critics, and journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging investigative broadcast reporting (accuracy, source verification, documentary authentication, and avoidance of political bias). Focuses on how to vet documentary evidence and reportage before publication or broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow basic journalistic principles
rubrics_metrics.description: CBS News failed to follow basic journalistic principles in the preparation and reporting of the September 8, 2004 broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify facts, corroborate sources, exercise skepticism, avoid letting a desired narrative override verification. The page treats adherence to fundamental journalistic methods as a baseline requirement; breach of these principles justifies internal review and public censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticate documents and verify provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: The documents on which the story was based supposedly came from the 'personal file' of Jerry Killian, but CBS was unable to identify a single witness to authenticate them; where did CBS News get them?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a clear chain of custody for documentary evidence; identify and obtain testimony from custodians or family members; do not rely on asserted provenance without independent corroboration; treat unexplained or inconsistent origin stories as a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use forensic document analysis where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Forensic document examiner Peter Tytell examined the documents and concluded they were produced on a computer using Times New Roman, not on a typewriter of the early 1970s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When typography, formatting, or other physical/document characteristics are central to authenticity, consult qualified forensic experts; examine fonts, spacing, and production methods in light of historical availability; give weight to sound forensic analysis in assessing authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate factual claims, dates, and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The memos' content contradicted basic facts (e.g., a memo dated August 18, 1973 implicated Staudt pressuring Hodges although Staudt retired on March 1, 1972).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check dates, personnel status, and contextual facts against contemporaneous records; inconsistencies between document content and known timelines undermine credibility; simple timeline checks can invalidate a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on a single, unvetted source
rubrics_metrics.description: CBS’s reliance on Bill Burkett as the source of the documents proved problematic: Burkett changed his story multiple times and ultimately admitted lying about where he obtained the documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not build a major report on the unverified claims of one source; seek independent corroboration and multiple, independent lines of evidence before airing explosive allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact and interview all relevant witnesses and potential sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Mapes made virtually no attempt to contact George Conn (alleged intermediary) or Mrs. Killian regarding whether Killian had personal files, used a typewriter, or had a secretary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make reasonable efforts to reach implicated parties, intermediaries, and family members to confirm existence of files and to test claims; failure to contact obvious witnesses is a lapse in basic reporting practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess source credibility and motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Burkett was described as a 'virulent Bush critic' and gave multiple, implausible explanations for the documents’ origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sources’ political views, possible motives, and consistency of accounts; changing or implausible explanations should reduce reliance on that source and trigger further vetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid publishing material timed or framed to influence elections
rubrics_metrics.description: A scandal of the first order: 'For the Record' was an attempt by a prominent organ of the mainstream media to influence the outcome of a presidential election with a false and fraudulent story just two months before Election Day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be especially rigorous with timing-sensitive stories that could affect public opinion or elections; avoid rushing or shaping reporting to maximize political impact; consider heightened verification standards in campaign seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rush to air without completing verification
rubrics_metrics.description: CBS scheduled a segment for late September but 'rushed it to air' on September 8, and the story began to fall apart within hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist pressure to broadcast before key verifications are complete; premature airing risks spreading falsehoods and causes greater reputational harm than delaying for thorough vetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not post potentially unauthenticated documents publicly before verification
rubrics_metrics.description: CBS News posted online PDF copies of four memos highlighted in the segment; once posted, commenters quickly challenged their authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid posting purported evidence in full until provenance and authenticity are established; releasing raw materials can magnify errors and enable quick public debunking if materials are suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission independent review and be transparent and accountable when errors occur
rubrics_metrics.description: CBS commissioned the Thornburgh–Boccardi independent panel; the station prefaced the story online with the panel’s conclusion that CBS failed to follow basic journalistic principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When major errors occur, commission independent panels, publish findings, apologize promptly and directly, and take appropriate personnel or institutional actions; transparent remediation is part of restoring credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use official contemporaneous records (personnel files, evaluations) to corroborate or refute claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The Thornburgh–Boccardi report quotes an authentic evaluation of Bush: 'Lt. Bush is an exceptional fighter interceptor pilot and officer,' contradicting the memos’ negative portrayal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek and compare contemporaneous official records and evaluations to the claims in questioned documents; authentic records can validate or refute narrative claims quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for confirmation bias and narrative-driven reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Mapes had been pursuing the story since 1999 and 'stands by the story' despite evidence; the piece suggests a predisposition to a particular narrative colored reporting choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and producers should be mindful of long-held agendas or expectations that may bias evidence selection; actively seek disconfirming evidence and let facts determine the narrative, not vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose conflicts of interest and relevant affiliations of interviewees
rubrics_metrics.description: Ben Barnes, interviewed by Rather, was vice chairman of Kerry’s national finance committee and a top fundraiser for Kerry; his implication of 'pull' constituted a problematic source connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear interviewees’ political or financial affiliations and consider how those affiliations affect credibility; disclose such connections to audiences and weigh them in editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate editorial oversight and institutional responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite the fiasco, Rather was never disciplined in connection with the story and later remained defiant; CBS’s handling (termination of Mapes, later departures) is discussed as institutional response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media organizations should have clear editorial oversight, escalation paths, and accountability mechanisms; post-mortem reviews should assess not only reporters but editorial and managerial decisions that allowed failures.
